item.title: Comment on Sunday assorted links by Hazel Meade
item.description:
4. I don't think Yarvin and his followers have ever really solved the problems faced by all autocracies throughout history. To start with, the information problem, but also the incentive structure - power corrupts. All centralized power systems trend towards the same problems with not having access to local information and the fact that in incentives of people in the hierarchy is to manipulate the centralized ruler, including centralized ruler's access to information, to their personal advantage. Disenchantment with the problems of democracies is not a solution. Democracy has it's own problems, yes - the main issue, identified by public choice theory is that concentrated benefits and dispersed costs allow small groups of people to lobby for, and obtain, specific benefits for themselves through political means. But this isn't a problem for only democracies. It's an innate problem with all forms of government (so far invented). Even monarchs have to play politics and please people who help keep them in power. A ruler who is not answerable to anyone (absolute monarch, dictator), might be able to overcome this issue, but there's no guarentee that his successor will be able to - the line of succession has to be secured through political support too. Anyway in reality, there aren't any absolute rulers. They have to have the support of the military command if nothing else.
At least liberal democracy represents a wary compromise between politics and economic efficiency. We aren't pure democrats, we have a bunch of rules limiting government, that allow individuals to be relatively free, which allows markets to do their magic processing local information and optimizing social utility. We could use a few more rules like that, but it won't likely be accomplished through a system like the one Yarvis is advocating.
